parts.note: Wimbledon Common is a large open public space in south-west London, an example of a common
a station is one's position or place, as in 'know your place'

explanation.surface: Wimbledon is described as a well-loved railway stop.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon suggests tennis, but here it is the open land of Wimbledon Common.
explanation.definitionFit: Something popular is widespread and ordinary, which is the sense of an everyday, familiar thing.

clue.text: Was in debt for ring, getting married

parts.note: a ring is round, the shape of the letter O
to get married is to wed

explanation.surface: Someone fell into debt to pay for a wedding ring.
explanation.definitionFit: To have been in debt is to have had money due to someone.

clue.text: Referee puts me on a diet that is new

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word new tells us the letters of these two words are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A sports official says the speaker must go on a new diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puts me on' places ME before the rest; 'that is new' rearranges A DIET into DIATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Referee is used as a verb: to settle a dispute between parties, as a go-between does.

clue.text: Crass f-football follower stands on his head

indicators.note: a down clue standing on its head is turned upside down, so the letters read in reverse order

parts.note: a football follower is a FAN; the stuttered f- adds an extra F in front

explanation.surface: A stammering, tasteless supporter does a headstand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stands on his head' turns FFAN upside down in the down light, giving NAFF.
explanation.definitionFit: Naff is British slang for tasteless or vulgar, much like crude or unrefined.

clue.text: Beware-! it may have high tars in it

definitions.meaning: a shouted warning to watch out, an imperative

definitions.text: it may have high tars in it
definitions.meaning: tars are sailors; a crow's nest high on a mast holds sailors keeping watch

explanation.walkthrough: 'tars' looks like the gunk in cigarettes, but in crosswords a tar is a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A warning shout to watch out, and a high watch post on a ship where sailors stand guard.

indicators.note: variety implies different arrangements, so the letters of the word acts are rearranged

explanation.surface: A stage show made up of variety turns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variety' suggests the music-hall acts of the surface, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A well-known Lloyd Webber stage musical based on T. S. Eliot's feline poems.

clue.text: Rush to look after sister, possibly

parts.note: to rush at something is to charge
to look after the sick is to nurse them

explanation.surface: Someone hurries off to care for a sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: In British hospitals a Sister is a senior nurse, which the surface hides as a sibling.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior ward nurse in Britain is called a Sister; a nurse in charge of a ward is an example.

clue.text: Caprine group gathers food all over the place

indicators.note: scattered all over the place, so the letters of these two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone collects provisions from everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Caprine means relating to goats, and a group of these animals kept together is a flock or herd.

parts.note: Suffolk Punches are a breed of heavy draught horse, so a man who buys and sells them trades punches, not blows

explanation.walkthrough: 'punches' suggests boxing blows; a Suffolk Punch is a British breed of heavy farm horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer in equines buys and sells animals such as the Suffolk Punch breed.

parts.note: a shooting-brake is an estate car, but read literally it is something that stops a gun from shooting

explanation.walkthrough: A shooting-brake is an old British name for an estate car; read literally it is a brake on shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: A gun's lock that prevents accidental firing acts as a brake on shooting.

clue.text: Chest to pose problem? Use this in diagnosis

indicators.note: a problem here is a puzzle to be worked out, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A doctor uses an instrument when the chest presents a difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'problem' reads as a medical difficulty, but it signals rearranging CHEST TO POSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor's listening instrument for heart and lungs is a standard tool in diagnosis.

definitions.meaning: in American English the bonnet of a car is called by a different word, the cover over the engine
Robin of Sherwood, the legendary English outlaw

explanation.walkthrough: 'bonnet' suggests a hat, but it is the British word for a car's engine cover.
explanation.definitionFit: The US word for a car's engine cover, and the surname of the Sherwood Forest outlaw Robin.

definitions.meaning: a ... cellar is the small dish holding table seasoning, not an underground room

explanation.walkthrough: A cellar here is a salt cellar, the small table container, not a basement.
explanation.definitionFit: An old seaman is called a salt, and the table seasoning is stored in a salt cellar.

clue.text: Bunch of ribbons worn as a favour

definitions.text: Bunch of ribbons worn as a favour

parts.words: Bunch of ribbons worn as a favour
parts.note: a gathered knot of ribbons pinned on to show support for a party or team, or awarded as a prize

explanation.definitionFit: A rosette is a circular knot of ribbon worn as a badge of support or awarded as a prize.

parts.note: piping is a decorative trim along the edge of fabric, so something piped has a trimmed border

explanation.walkthrough: 'Piped over the border' suggests pipers marching into Scotland; it means trimmed along the edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A garment trimmed with piping has a decorative strip along its margin.

clue.text: Take on more fellows in a tug, at sea

indicators.note: the word in tells us one piece is placed inside the other
at sea means confused or all over the place, so the letters of a tug are rearranged

parts.note: fellows are men

explanation.surface: A tugboat takes on extra crew while out on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' turns A TUG into AUGT, which MEN goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To augment is to increase or add to, so taking on more extends what you have.

indicators.note: an environment surrounds whatever is in it, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: arid means very dry
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A harsh, chilly wind blows in a parched landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrid describes a sharp, harsh, unpleasant taste or smell.

indicators.note: the letters are taken from within these words, running across them

explanation.surface: A command issued by a tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is spelt out inside 'thE DICTator'.
explanation.definitionFit: An edict is an official decree or proclamation, a command from authority.

definitions.meaning: leftover pieces, such as the last bits of a loaf or roll of cloth
goals or aims, as in 'the means to an end'

explanation.definitionFit: Leftover bits and pieces, and the aims or goals one strives for.

clue.text: Beginner in mountain district left out

indicators.note: out tells us a letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: the Tyrol is an Alpine region of Austria and Italy

explanation.surface: A novice is in the Alps but has been excluded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' takes the L away from TYROL.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyro is a novice or learner who has only just started out.

clue.text: Warmish sort of diet includes a pint

indicators.note: includes tells us one piece holds the other inside it
sort of means a version of, so the letters of diet are rearranged

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for pint

explanation.surface: A lukewarm kind of diet allows a pint of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges DIET into TEID, which 'includes' P.
explanation.definitionFit: Lukewarm or slightly warm, neither hot nor cold.

parts.note: a rig on which engines or machines are run under test, a bed being a base or bench

explanation.definitionFit: A rig or platform used to run trials on engines and new equipment.

clue.text: Pluck needed to find treasure in river

indicators.note: in tells us one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and also one on the England-Wales border
a plum is a prize or something highly valued

explanation.surface: Courage is needed to find hidden treasure in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pluck' reads as courage, but it is the verb meaning to strip feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: To pluck a bird is to strip off its feathers.

clue.text: Without thorns, duramen can be worked

indicators.note: working material reshapes it, so the letters of duramen are rearranged

explanation.surface: Thornless heartwood is easy to craft.
explanation.walkthrough: Duramen is the heartwood of a tree; 'unarmed' is the botanical term for a plant with no thorns or prickles.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany a plant bearing no spines or prickles is described as having no weapons.

indicators.note: strange signals that the letters of dialect are put into an odd order

explanation.surface: An odd local speech found near an estuary.
explanation.definitionFit: A delta is the fan of land at a river's outlet, so the adjective describes things related to it.

parts.note: a bishop's see is his diocese

explanation.surface: A diocese suits a prophet well.
explanation.definitionFit: A seer foresees the future, like an oracle.

clue.text: Fun for students, a kind of Indian music

parts.note: RAG is British student charity fun, as in rag week

explanation.surface: Students enjoy themselves with classical music from India.
explanation.walkthrough: Rag week is a British university tradition of fundraising stunts.
explanation.definitionFit: A raga is a melodic framework in Indian classical music.

clue.text: Eyesore you once found on street

parts.note: ye is an old form of you

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned person finds an ugly sight in the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eyesore' means an ugly sight, but is read literally as a sore on the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid, a literally sore eye.

parts.note: SC is an abbreviation for science
to be up is to be in residence at university, especially Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: Porgy, from the opera, goes off to study science at college.
explanation.definitionFit: The scup is a North American sea bream, also known as a porgy.

parts.note: a saloon is a type of car, a sedan

explanation.surface: A fellow called Mark is in a bar on Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saloon' suggests a bar, but in British English it is a car with a closed body.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is the lasting mark left by a healed wound.

parts.note: rabbit is hunted as game
punch is a mixed drink often with spices

explanation.surface: A karate blow, followed by a meal of game and mulled drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbit punch is a sharp blow to the back of the neck.

parts.note: a candle gives light
a berry is a small fruit

explanation.surface: A bush whose fruit is low in calories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'light fruit' suggests low-calorie produce; the berries of this shrub give wax for candles.
explanation.definitionFit: The wax myrtle, a bush whose berries yield candle wax, is known by this name.
